options.why: Confuses collision frequency with a loss of particle speed.

options.why: Believes the same temperature means the same average speed for every gas.

payload.stem: A sample of nitrogen gas in a rigid container is heated from 200 K to 400 K. A student claims that the average kinetic energy of the molecules doubles, but the average speed of the molecules increases by a factor of less than 2. Which statement best justifies the claim?

options.text: The attractions between the liquid molecules become much weaker as the sample is heated, so the molecules of the liquid no longer attract one another at all as they are heated.

options.text: Every molecule in the liquid gains exactly the same extra kinetic energy, so all of the molecules are able to escape at once and the pressure rises very sharply.
options.why: Believes all molecules have the same energy and all can escape.

options.text: Heating creates additional molecules of the substance in the container, so the pressure of the gas rises whether or not any more liquid evaporates at all.
options.why: Believes heating creates new molecules.

payload.stem: A student claims that, at constant temperature, doubling the surface area of a liquid in a sealed container does not change the equilibrium vapor pressure of the liquid. Which statement best justifies the claim?

options.text: Only the molecules at the center of the liquid can escape into the gas, so the surface area of the liquid is irrelevant to the rate of evaporation.
options.why: Believes molecules in the interior, not at the surface, escape.

options.text: A larger surface area doubles both the rate of evaporation and the rate of condensation, so the pressure at which the two rates are equal stays the same.
options.why: At equilibrium the rates of evaporation and condensation are equal; both scale with the surface area, so the equilibrium vapor pressure is set by the temperature and the intermolecular forces.

options.text: The extra surface area cools the liquid by exactly the amount needed to keep the equilibrium vapor pressure from changing as the surface is enlarged.
options.why: Believes evaporative cooling cancels a surface-area effect.

options.text: The vapor pressure depends only on the volume of the container, so changing the surface area of the liquid cannot have any effect on the vapor pressure of the liquid.
options.why: Believes vapor pressure depends on the container volume and not on temperature and forces.

facts: surface area does not change equilibrium vapor pressure

payload.stem: Honey flows much more easily after it is warmed in a water bath. Which particle-level model best explains the decrease in viscosity?

options.text: Warming raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so more of them overcome the attractions to neighbors and slide past one another, lowering the viscosity.
options.why: Higher kinetic energy lets more molecules overcome the intermolecular attractions, so the molecules slide past one another more easily and the viscosity drops.

options.text: Warming breaks the covalent bonds inside the molecules, so the molecules become much smaller and are able to flow past one another more easily than they could before.
options.why: Confuses breaking intermolecular attractions with breaking covalent bonds.

options.text: Warming spreads the molecules apart until the liquid behaves like a gas with no attractions left, so the viscosity of the liquid falls to a value of zero.
options.why: Believes a warmed liquid becomes a gas with no attractions.

options.text: Warming makes each molecule heavier, so the liquid moves downhill faster under gravity and the measured viscosity of the liquid becomes smaller as a result.
options.why: Believes warming changes the mass of a molecule.

payload.stem: The viscosity of liquid water is measured at three temperatures: 1.31 mPa·s at 10 °C, 0.65 mPa·s at 40 °C, and 0.40 mPa·s at 70 °C. Which particle-level model best explains this trend?

options.text: Warming makes each molecule heavier, so the liquid moves downhill faster under gravity and the measured viscosity of the liquid becomes smaller as a result.
options.why: Believes warming changes the mass of a molecule.

options.text: Warming raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so more of them overcome the attractions to neighbors and slide past one another, lowering the viscosity.
options.why: Higher kinetic energy lets more molecules overcome the intermolecular attractions, so the molecules slide past one another more easily and the viscosity drops.

options.text: Warming spreads the molecules apart until the liquid behaves like a gas with no attractions left, so the viscosity of the liquid falls to a value of zero.
options.why: Believes a warmed liquid becomes a gas with no attractions.

options.text: Warming breaks the covalent bonds inside the molecules, so the molecules become much smaller and are able to flow past one another more easily than they could before.
options.why: Confuses breaking intermolecular attractions with breaking covalent bonds.

facts: water viscosity falls from 1.31 to 0.40 mPa·s between 10 and 70 °C

payload.stem: Sulfur trioxide, SO₃, and the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻, each have three oxygen atoms bonded to a central sulfur atom. Which statement correctly compares their shapes?

options.text: SO₃ is trigonal planar because sulfur has three electron domains and no lone pair, while SO₃²⁻ is trigonal pyramidal because sulfur has four domains with one lone pair.
options.why: SO₃: (6 + 0 − 0)/2 = 3 domains, no lone pair, trigonal planar. SO₃²⁻: (6 + 0 + 2)/2 = 4 domains, three bonds and one lone pair, trigonal pyramidal.

options.text: Both are trigonal planar because the central sulfur atom in each species is bonded to three oxygen atoms, and bonded atoms alone decide the shape of each species.
options.why: Ignores the lone pair on the central atom.

options.text: SO₃ is trigonal pyramidal and SO₃²⁻ is trigonal planar because the extra negative charge removes the lone pair from the sulfur atom in the sulfite ion.
options.why: Reverses the effect of the added electrons.

options.text: Both are trigonal pyramidal because a sulfur atom that is bonded to oxygen always carries a lone pair of electrons, so each species has the same trigonal pyramid shape in the end.
options.why: Believes sulfur always has a lone pair.

payload.stem: The carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, and the chlorate ion, ClO₃⁻, each have three oxygen atoms bonded to a central atom. Which statement correctly compares their shapes?

options.text: Both are trigonal pyramidal because a central atom that is bonded to oxygen always carries a lone pair of electrons, so each ion has the same trigonal pyramid shape in the end.
options.why: Believes every central atom bonded to oxygen has a lone pair.

options.text: CO₃²⁻ is trigonal planar because carbon has three electron domains and no lone pair, while ClO₃⁻ is trigonal pyramidal because chlorine has four domains with one lone pair.
options.why: CO₃²⁻: (4 + 0 + 2)/2 = 3 domains, no lone pair, trigonal planar. ClO₃⁻: (7 + 0 + 1)/2 = 4 domains, three bonds and one lone pair, trigonal pyramidal.

options.text: CO₃²⁻ is trigonal pyramidal and ClO₃⁻ is trigonal planar because the ion with the larger negative charge must be the one that carries the lone pair on its central atom.
options.why: Believes the larger charge decides which ion has the lone pair.

options.text: Both are trigonal planar because the central atom in each ion is bonded to three oxygen atoms, and bonded atoms alone decide the shape of each ion.
options.why: Ignores the lone pair on the central atom.
